description: Space Startup is a team of teenage students passionate about space exploration. By examining NASA Mars rover engineering, historical achievements, and scientific findings, our team transforms planetary mission data into innovative concepts for future space exploration.
summary:
Mars Rover Legacy is an interactive video game that takes players through the history of three NASA Mars rovers: Sojourner, Spirit, and Opportunity.
Players begin with the first rover, Sojourner, and complete its assigned mission tasks. They experience how the rover landed on Mars, explore the places it visited, operate its scientific instruments, and discover what it taught us about the Red Planet. Each mission concludes once the explorer ceases operation, mimicking the actual historical cause of its end on Mars.
When a rover's mission ends, the next rover unlocks, introducing more advanced technology, new scientific goals, and new challenges. Players learn how each rover contributed to our understanding of Mars, why its mission ended, and how its discoveries helped prepare humanity for future exploration.
At the end of each chapter, players can also suggest creative ideas to NASA for improving future Mars rovers and missions.
The goal is to make the history of Mars exploration fun and interactive while helping players understand how each rover's discoveries bring us closer to answering the question: Could Mars have supported life?
details:
Mars Rover Legacy is an educational video game that lets players live the full missions of NASA's first three Mars rovers — Sojourner (1997), Spirit (2004), and Opportunity (2004) — the machines that now sit abandoned on Mars. All three chapters are linked in one game: finishing one rover's story unlocks the next.

In each chapter, the player watches the rover's real airbag landing — the lander bounces down, its airbags deflate, and its petals open (our game even uses NASA's real photo of the Pathfinder lander at the moment the rover rolls out). The player then drives the rover across scrolling Mars landscapes with one arrow key. Along the way, the rover stops at three real discovery sites per mission — Barnacle Bill, Yogi, and Scooby-Doo for Sojourner; the RAT-drilled rock Humphrey, the silica soil of Silica Valley, and the layered plateau Home Plate for Spirit; and Eagle Crater's "blueberries," Victoria Crater, and the gypsum vein at Endeavour Crater for Opportunity — and each stop opens a short science card explaining what the rover found there. A sol counter climbs to each rover's true mission length (83, 2,208, and 5,111 sols), and each chapter ends the way the real mission ended. At the end of every chapter, players are asked, "What would YOU improve for the next rover?" and type in their own ideas. Original music and sound effects — a landing theme, travel music, a discovery chime, and a battery power-down sound — carry the story from landing to last signal.


The game turns space history into hands-on play. Instead of memorizing facts, players discover them the way the rovers did: hematite "blueberries" that prove Mars once had liquid water, silica soil left by hot springs or steam vents, and a gypsum vein that shows the water was once gentle enough for life. It keeps the stories of retired spacecraft alive for a new generation, runs free in any web browser with no downloads, and uses controls simple enough for elementary and middle school students.


We want players to stop seeing abandoned rovers as junk and start seeing them as storytellers. Every discarded machine on Mars carries a story of exploration, problem-solving, and discovery. If our game makes students curious about those stories — and makes them think like engineers by contributing their own improvement ideas — then the rovers' missions are still teaching, decades after their last signals.


The game was built in Scratch (block-based coding) on scratch.mit.edu, so it runs in a browser on any laptop or Chromebook. Our research came from NASA and JPL mission pages and records. The artwork combines hand-drawn vector art with real NASA photography (the Pathfinder lander) and Mars landscape images. All music and sound effects were composed and synthesized by our team using Python. We also produced a short narrated intro video for the project. No special hardware was needed — just computers and a browser.


We tell the story through gameplay, not text. The player doesn't read about the rovers — they drive their lives: bouncing down in airbags, rolling out of the lander, crossing real terrain, and feeling each mission's ending, from Sojourner's fading battery to Spirit's final stop in the Troy sand trap to Opportunity's last days in the great dust storm of 2018 (with the power-down sound to match). Mixing a real NASA photograph into a cartoon world makes the history feel present and true. And the "Ideas for NASA" moment turns every player from an audience into a designer of the next rover.


Historical accuracy came first: every date, sol count, landing site, and discovery was checked against NASA sources, because these are real missions that deserve to be told correctly. We also designed for our audience — young students — with one-key driving, short science cards, and bright, friendly art and music. We chose to be honest about the endings: the rovers' stories are sad, but we present them as hopeful, because each rover far outlived its planned mission (Sojourner lasted 12 times longer than planned; Opportunity, nearly 15 years instead of 90 days). Finally, we kept the project accessible — free, browser-based, and playable on school computers — so any student can step onto Mars.
